An archiphoneme is an ordinary phoneme whose spelling the plain form carries. Author its sound rule separately. Trial the unaffected forms and the forms the prohibitions exclude, as well as forms changed by the rule; a structural replacement alone does not prove parse preservation.

## One form blocked after one form of another affix

Sometimes one form of an affix is wrong only after one particular form of an earlier affix: a stative `-lik` fits after an applicative `-o` but not after `-e`, while `-k` fits after both. Create an allomorph prohibition with the CLI verb `compose-author-adhoc-prohibition`, which MCP offers as `motif_author_adhoc_prohibition` (kind `allomorph`; the later form as `first`, the earlier form as `rest`, adjacency `adjacent-to-right`). The parser drops only that pair of forms. Use it between forms of different entries: in an inflectional template an entry fills one slot, so a rule between two forms of the same entry would never fire there. To choose between forms of one entry, give each its own environment, or put the narrowest first and the general form last.

## Every sound except some, and a zero form chosen by class

A natural class is a fixed list of sounds (or of feature values), and FieldWorks has no complement or negated class. A project file can hold a negated feature value (LibLCM stores one), but FieldWorks' parser loader cannot read it and FieldWorks offers no way to make one, so do not rely on it; the grammar check warns (`grammar.negated-feature-value`) when a project holds one. For "every consonant except `<sound>`", list the sounds wanted (author the class with `motif_add_natural_class`) and add a sound to it when the inventory grows. A zero affix that should depend on the stem's class, not on the sounds around it, takes `inflectionClasses` (`motif_add_lexical_entry`, or `motif_add_alternate_form` for a form of an existing entry) and no environment; a stem of any other class gets no reading from it.

## Circumfix parts

Each part of a circumfix keeps its own environment on the real parser (a real-parser test, `RealParserCircumfixEnvironmentTests`, authors `ma-` with `-ang` after a consonant and `-x` after a vowel as two circumfix entries, each part with its own environment, and the parser chooses by the stem's last sound; the prefix part's environment is tested at the stem start and the suffix part's at the stem end). A part whose environment names the other part's side can never hold, so give each part a context on its own side of the stem. Run a Trial with the words each way: a missing half, the wrong linker and a stem the prefix environment excludes all stay unparsed.

## Check with a Trial

After a composer can express the change, include attested words from each sound context and words just outside those contexts. Confirm each variant appears where expected and that the unrestricted form does not win before a narrower variant. Include words that should remain unchanged.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the evidence does not show whether the variants share a morpheme or what sound defines the environment. Use real project forms: “I found `<attested form A>` before `<observed sound class A>` and `<attested form B>` before `<observed sound class B>`. Does `<variant>` also occur before `<attested sound C>`, or is that a separate morpheme?” Replace bracketed items with forms read from this project; label any unobserved form as a prediction.

## Common wrong choices

- A separate entry for each variant of one morpheme.
- An environment broader than the evidence, or an unrestricted form placed before narrower ones.
- Listing variants for a regular sound change across many forms; a phonological rule fits that better.
- A new entry for each pattern-based form of one affix, or a plain alternate form for a pattern change; use `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`.

entries.title: Feature-conditioned template slots
entries.description: A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.
entries.helpPage:
# Feature-conditioned template slots

A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.

## Encode the pattern

- Declare a feature and its values when the distinction has grammatical meaning the rest of the analysis needs to see.
- Put a noun's gender pair (for example 7/8) on the stem's grammatical analysis and its number on the class prefix's required features: each reading shows the prefix's number, the stem's gender filters which prefixes fit, and a number requirement never filters a stem that lacks one.
- Make two affixes in different slots agree (a subject marker and a relative marker, say) by giving both the same feature value in their required features: the parser keeps each affix's requirement on the word, so a pair that disagrees has no analysis. Use one feature whose values are the agreement groups, and give an affix that serves two groups one entry per group. Do not use this where the second affix agrees with something else, such as a suffix relative that agrees with the object.
- Put the supported value on the stem's grammatical analysis. Restrict an inflectional affix to its required feature values, then link it to the appropriate slot.
- Keep the template for the shared order of positions. Use separate templates only when forms have different required positions; use an optional slot only when that position may truly be absent.
- A template cannot be limited to a stem inflection class: FieldWorks ties a template to a category and the parser reads no class on it. To give one class its own affixes, restrict each affix in that template's slots to the class (`inflectionClasses` on `motif_add_lexical_entry` or `motif_add_alternate_form`, or `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes`) or require a feature value on the affix. A stem of another class then finds no complete template; an optional slot lets it pass without the affix.
- Do not use an arbitrary inflection class for a value that must participate in agreement. Do not let every affix compete in the slot without the feature restrictions the data supports.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read features, feature values, inflection classes and templates. `motif_add_inflection_feature` declares a closed morphosyntactic feature with its named values, and `motif_add_inflection_class` creates a category-owned class that can be assigned to a stem MSA through `motif_add_lexical_entry`. `motif_add_affix_slot` and `motif_add_affix_template` create the category-owned positions and their order. `motif_add_feature_structure` creates an empty feature structure on an existing or earlier-staged stem, inflectional affix or derivational affix MSA (a derivational affix takes side from or to), refusing an occupied slot. Use its returned exact structure identity with `motif_add_feature_value` to require a closed-feature specification, optionally selecting an existing value belonging to that exact feature. Inflectional affix selections are requirements on the word, not output features; their definitions must belong to the current morphosyntactic feature system and any declared structure type. A stem's values remain separate from the affix's requirements. `motif_remove_feature_value` removes one feature's specification from a stem or affix structure, including a derivational affix's From or To structure.

## Check with a Trial

Try words with each attested value and a contrasting value. Confirm the right affix appears for each value, the wrong affix does not, and a word with missing or incompatible information does not acquire an unsupported analysis. Include negative words and any known exceptions.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when it is unclear whether a contrast is grammatical agreement or arbitrary lexical grouping, or which value belongs to a form. Use attested forms: “`<attested form A>` takes `<affix A>` and is marked `<observed value A>`; `<attested form B>` takes `<affix B>`. Does `<attested form C>` have value `<value A>` or `<value B>`?” Replace bracketed items with project evidence and ask only the question that distinguishes the encodings.

## Common wrong choices

- An arbitrary inflection class for a value that must agree with other words.
- Letting every affix compete for a slot without feature restrictions the data supports.
- A separate affix or slot per feature value.

entries.title: Segmental nasal assimilation
entries.description: A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.
entries.helpPage:
# Segmental nasal assimilation

A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.

## Encode the pattern

- First establish the underlying nasal and the contexts in which its surface form changes.
- Use phonological features or natural classes to describe the nasal, the conditioning sounds and the change. Keep the context narrow enough to exclude unrelated nasals and consonants.
- Use a regular segmental rule for a sound change across forms. Record rule order and whether the pattern applies simultaneously or iteratively when that affects the evidence.
- Do not duplicate a whole affix for each place of articulation when one rule accounts for the alternation. Do not write a rule that changes every nasal merely because some nasals assimilate.
- Treat deletion, exceptional spellings or lexical restrictions as separate decisions when the data supports them; do not hide them in an over-broad assimilation rule.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read phonemes, natural classes and phonological rules. `motif_add_phoneme`, `motif_add_natural_class` and `motif_add_phonological_rule` create the sound inventory, reusable sound classes and regular rules. A rule intent names existing phonemes or natural classes in its input, output and contexts. `motif_edit_phonological_rule` changes a rule in place, `motif_order_phonological_rules` reorders rules, `motif_set_phonological_rule_disabled` turns one off or on, and `motif_delete_phonological_rule` removes one. A context item may be optional or repeated. Input and Output each accept up to eight phoneme or natural-class items in order, and may have different lengths. A segment-list natural class in the Output does not choose a member; it applies only the features its members share, and the input keeps its own value for the rest. An aligned feature-class Output changes the named features on the matched segment and preserves the rest; see [Feature rules](guide:encoding/feature-rules). Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` to get the rule's `intent` for an edit's `expected` guard. `motif_add_phonological_feature` and `motif_add_phonological_feature_value` define the phonological features and their values, `motif_edit_phoneme_features` sets them on phonemes, and `motif_edit_natural_class_features` changes the feature constraints of a natural class; a class by features can be created with `motif_add_natural_class` (`features`). A nasal that changes with its neighbour is often an archiphoneme, a phoneme only the underlying form carries (`motif_guide(topic="archiphonemes")`). `motif_add_affix_process` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` express a substitution as pattern-based forms of one affix instead. `motif_guide(topic="conditioned-allomorphs")` describes the related case where the evidence instead supports stored conditioned variants.

## Order the rules

Rules apply one after another, and a later rule sees the output of the earlier ones. A chain such as a place rule (a class becomes a nasal after the archiphoneme) followed by a deletion rule (the archiphoneme drops before a nasal) and an elsewhere rule (the archiphoneme becomes the velar nasal) works only in that order. If the elsewhere rule comes first, the archiphoneme is gone before the others see it and the words get no analysis. Reorder instead of rewriting; test a word for each branch. A segment-list natural class can also be used without phonological features. Feature-class rules require the relevant features and represented counterpart phonemes.

## Check with a Trial

Include attested forms for each conditioning place, forms where the nasal should stay unchanged, and negative words that should not become valid. Check that each output matches the evidence and that rule ordering does not alter unrelated segments.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the forms do not decide whether the change is assimilation, a stored allomorph or a lexical exception. Build one contrast from actual project forms: “In `<attested form A>`, the nasal is before `<observed sound A>`; in `<attested form B>`, it is before `<observed sound B>`. Does the same morpheme occur before `<attested sound C>`, and what form do speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with evidence and distinguish observed forms from predictions.

## Common wrong choices

- Duplicating an affix for each place of articulation when one rule explains the alternation.
- An unconstrained affix process for a nasal change may require substantial parser work. Several processes kept as allomorphs of one Verb-only entry (the restriction comes from the entry's grammatical info; the composer has no category input), with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, stopped no words with compounding off.
- A rule that changes every nasal because only some assimilate.

When only some prefixes substitute, the change is conditioned by the morpheme, not by sound alone. Cebuano is an example: Wolff treats substitution at the paN-, maN-, naN- and hiN- boundary as systematic (p, b become m; t, d, s become n; k and glottal stop become ng; l becomes ngl or nl, both accepted), while ning- and ming- keep k (ningkubit, mingkuyánap). Put the substituting forms on one entry as process allomorphs with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, not in a phonological rule that would also apply to the prefixes that keep the consonant.

entries.title: A supported finding of no inflection
entries.description: A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.
entries.helpPage:
# A supported finding of no inflection

A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.

## Encode the pattern

- Compare the same lexemes across the grammatical contexts at issue. Check representative words and exceptions before deciding that there is no inflection.
- Leave out affix entries, slots and templates for a category when the evidence shows no inflectional form change there.
- Keep lexical meaning, part of speech and any grammatical features that the analysis actually needs. A language can have grammatical distinctions without marking them by affixes.
- Do not add a null affix or empty slot just to represent an assumed default. Do not conclude “no inflection” from one unchanged word or from missing data.

## Motif support

`motif_lexicon`, `motif_grammar` and `motif_word` can show the forms and analyses already recorded. `motif_add_lexeme_form` can edit an existing form, and `motif_add_feature_structure` can add an empty structure to an existing stem analysis; neither is needed to record the absence of an affix. No grammar composer is required to leave an unsupported affix out.

## Check with a Trial

Do not use a Trial as proof that an affix does not exist. If a Proposal changes nearby grammar, include representative unchanged forms and negative words in `motif_trial`; confirm they remain unchanged and do not gain analyses from the new rule. If there is no change to propose, report the evidence without creating an empty Proposal.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the project lacks enough comparable forms to separate no inflection from missing or unrecorded data. Use attested examples: “`<attested form A>` and `<attested form B>` have the same form in the contexts recorded here. Are these the same lexeme in contrasting `<grammatical contexts>`, and is there another form speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with observed project data; do not state the absence as settled until the comparison is supported.

## Common wrong choices

- Inventing an affix or template because another language marks the distinction.
- Approximating a missing composer with unrelated edits.

entries.title: Prefix and suffix slots
entries.description: A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.
entries.helpPage:
# Prefix and suffix slots

A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.

## Encode the pattern

- Keep one affix entry for one morpheme, with its prefix or suffix morph type, form and grammatical analysis.
- Put inflectional affixes in slots owned by the part of speech they apply to. Put those slots in the template in the order speakers use them.
- Mark a slot optional only when that grammatical position may truly be absent. Use separate templates when forms have different required positions.
- Do not make a new affix entry for each stem that takes the same affix. Do not use one broad slot for affixes with different grammatical jobs.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read categories, templates and slots. `motif_add_lexical_entry` creates one entry and one sense with a structured MSA: use an inflectional MSA for a slot-filling affix, or a derivational MSA with both its source and destination categories. `motif_add_affix_slot` creates a category-owned slot and can assign existing inflectional MSAs; `motif_add_affix_template` creates the ordered prefix and suffix slots. Use returned entity ids in later calls or batches after the creating call completes. Batch intents may reference only ids from earlier completed calls or batches; declare operation ordering and dependencies in the intent data, since array position alone does not establish them.

## Restricting which stems an affix attaches to

Where the restriction goes depends on the kind of affix, because FieldWorks' parser reads it from different places.

- Inflectional grammatical info: restrict the affix form to inflection classes. `motif_add_alternate_form` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` take `inflectionClasses`, and `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes` changes them later. FieldWorks reads the form's Inflection Classes for inflectional grammatical info only.
- Derivational grammatical info: use the `motif_edit_derivational_affix_restriction` MCP tool or `compose-edit-derivational-affix-restriction` CLI verb to set or clear its From Inflection Class and, optionally, set From Exception Features and To Exception Features (the features the derived stem receives); `alsoMsas` applies the same change to many affixes in one intent, and `compose-add-exception-features` adds features to many derivational affixes at once (`"side":"to"` for the To set). An affix process such as reduplication takes the same restriction, since the features sit on its grammatical info. FieldWorks reads those fields from the derivational grammatical info. Form inflection classes do not restrict a derivational analysis, so a mixed entry can use both paths for their corresponding analyses. If an entry has no inflectional grammatical info, Motif refuses form `inflectionClasses` and names the derivational restriction tool.

An unmarked stem does not take a derivational affix restricted to a class: only stems assigned that class do. Assign the class to the stems first, or the affix will stop applying to every stem you meant it for.

## Check with a Trial

Include words that should take each affix and words that should not. Check that the affixes appear in the intended order, that required slots are filled, and that unrelated words do not gain extra parses. A Trial checks the Proposal; it does not create grammar objects.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the forms do not show whether an affix is required, optional or ordered relative to another affix. Build one question from attested words: “I found `<attested form A>` with `<affix A>` and `<attested form B>` with `<affix B>`. In `<attested context C>`, should both affixes occur, and in what order?” Replace each bracketed item with evidence from this project.

## Common wrong choices

- An affix entry per stem, or one broad slot for affixes with different jobs.
- An unclassified affix when an inflectional or derivational analysis with a slot fits.
- An ad hoc prohibition for an order a template can express.
- Inflection classes on a form when the entry has no inflectional grammatical info; restrict its derivational grammatical info instead.

entries.title: Work through one grammar question
entries.description: Start by learning what the saved project and words already show. Make one small Proposal, try it against observed examples and counterexamples, and hand the measured result to the linguist.
entries.helpPage:
# Work through one grammar question

Start by learning what the saved project and words already show. Make one small Proposal, try it against observed examples and counterexamples, and hand the measured result to the linguist.

## Inspect

- Use `motif_list_projects`. If the intended project is not Known, ask for its exact existing `.fwdata` path if
  needed, call `motif_open` with that path, then pass it as `project` on later calls. Use the Known project name or
  recorded path for other calls.
- Read `motif_overview`, then `motif_grammar` and `motif_lexicon` for the relevant objects and forms.
- Use `motif_word` for the linguist's recorded analysis and `motif_try_word` to see how the current grammar handles a form.
- Read the guide for the phenomenon: `motif_guide` over MCP, or `motif help guide:encoding/<topic> --full` from the CLI (`motif help` lists the topics). Check whether Motif has a composer for every object the encoding needs.

## Draft one small Proposal

- State one linguistic claim and the project evidence for it.
- Use `motif_start_proposal` and the available semantic composers that fit the claim. New grammar objects include parts of speech, lexical entries with one sense and MSA, inflection features and classes, stem names, affix slots and templates, plus phonemes, natural classes, environments and phonological rules.
- Use `motif_compose_batch` to stage related intents together. Supply each as a `verb` and structured `intent` object, with an optional `citation`. Use entity ids returned by earlier completed calls or batches; an intent that needs a newly created entity's returned id belongs in a later call or batch.
- Keep the Proposal to one related change. If a required composer is missing, say which encoding cannot be made and why; do not approximate it with unrelated edits.

## A stem two obligatory rules both want

Phonological rules in FieldWorks are obligatory, and there is no optional rule and no per-stem rule order. When two rules each need their own exception feature and the first removes what the second needs (syncope bleeding a d-to-r rule), a stem tagged for both surfaces only the first outcome. This is Black's route, not an optional rule: exception features that gate rules (Black 2.1.6, and 6.1.2.2.2, "Rule applies only with certain properties"), tried before any ad hoc rule. Give the stem one analysis per outcome, each tagged for one rule only:

1. Tag the existing analysis for the first rule with `motif_edit_exception_features` (`compose-edit-exception-features`).
2. Add a second analysis tagged for the other rule with `motif_add_morphosyntax_analysis`, giving `msa.exceptionFeatures` and a `gloss` for its sense. The original sense stays on the original analysis and the gloss adds a second sense, so an entry with one sense ends with two; each analysis needs a sense of its own, because a sense points at exactly one analysis and FieldWorks removes an analysis no sense uses; one sense cannot serve both. Make the gloss say what the sense is for, in the form `<original gloss> (second analysis: <rule or form it carries>)`, for example `to open (second analysis: d-to-r form)`. FieldWorks shows this sense in the entry beside the original, and a person can merge or reword it there. Do not move the only sense with `senses`: the old analysis would be dropped and the split becomes a retag.
3. Run a Trial with both surface forms and a word neither rule should make. Split only stems whose second form is attested: each split costs one more parse path for that stem.

A form that may surface either way takes a third analysis with no tag. A whole-word variant listed as its own entry also works, but it misses the productive forms built on the stem.

## Name an object by its form, not its id

An id is a GUID, and an object a Proposal creates gets a new one every time that Proposal is composed, so a plan written against one project (a private copy, say) names ids that do not exist in another (the live project). Any string in an intent that starts with `lookup:` is read as a name and replaced by the id of the object in the project the Draft is composed against, including one an earlier step of the same Draft created: `lookup:entry:ika-` (an entry by lexeme form, with the affix hyphen to pick the affix; add `|gloss` to separate homographs), `lookup:sense:FORM|GLOSS`, `lookup:msa:FORM|GLOSS` (the sense's grammatical info), `lookup:phoneme:GRAPHEME`, `lookup:category:NAME`, `lookup:phonological-feature:NAME` and `lookup:phonological-feature-value:FEATURE|VALUE`. Phonological feature and value names or abbreviations match exactly in the default analysis writing system. A name that matches nothing, or more than one object, is refused with the ids of the objects it matched. Stored Drafts keep the resolved ids, so a Draft replays the same way afterwards.

## Try it, then ask or defer

- Run `motif_dry_run`, then `motif_trial` with attested positive forms, contrasting forms and words that should not parse.
- Read the Trial summary in order: negatives now parsing, positives lost, unfinished cases, other changes, counts.
- Use `motif_difference` with the stored Difference id and category to page through exact before and after analyses. Unfinished cases prove no absence.
- If evidence leaves competing analyses that change the Proposal, ask one question using attested forms. Defer when the linguist cannot yet answer it.
- Revise and repeat the Trial after a meaningful change. Do not describe an unmeasured change as a parser improvement.

## Hand off

- When the Dry Run and Trial support the change, call `motif_finalize_proposal` and tell the linguist what evidence was checked and what remains uncertain.
- The linguist reviews the Proposal in Motif and decides whether to apply it. Do not claim that it was applied.

## CLI equivalents

The guides name MCP tools. From the CLI, use the matching `motif` command; run `motif help <command> --full` for its flags.

| MCP tool | CLI command |
|---|---|
| `motif_list_projects`, `motif_open` | `motif open <fwdata>` |
| `motif_overview` | `motif overview` |
| `motif_grammar`, `motif_lexicon` | `motif grammar read --kind <kind>` (`lexical_entry` for the lexicon) |
| `motif_texts` | `motif texts list` |
| `motif_word` | `motif word-context --word <word>` |
| `motif_try_word` | `motif trace --word <word>` |
| `motif_start_proposal` | `motif new --draft <name>` |
| the add and edit tools, such as `motif_add_phonological_rule` or `motif_edit_allomorph_condition` | the `compose-author-*` and `compose-edit-*` commands, such as `motif compose-author-phonological-rule` |
| `motif_compose_batch` | `motif compose-batch` |
| `motif_finalize_proposal` | `motif finalize` |
| `motif_dry_run`, `motif_trial` | `motif dry-run`, `motif trial` (add `--wait` to read the result) |
| `motif_difference` | `motif difference produce` |
| `motif_guide` | `motif help guide:encoding/<topic> --full` |

## Composer notes

- **Exception features are set as a whole list.** `compose-edit-exception-features` replaces the exact list on a stem or an inflectional affix. To add a feature to an entry that already has some, read its current features first and send the merged list: the old ones plus the new one. Sending only the new one removes the rest. `compose-add-exception-features` adds without replacing, to stems, inflectional affixes and derivational affixes (From Exception Features by default, To with `"side":"to"`).
- **Bulk retype uses `compose-batch`.** One file with an intent per stem (`compose-set-stem-part-of-speech`) stages hundreds in one Draft and one Proposal. `grammar-check` lists the likely stems as `lexicon.stem-typed-as-content-word`, with duplicate entries and affixes whose hyphen is on the wrong side; the report changes nothing.
- **Reaching an object made earlier in the same batch.** Give the step an `as` label, then write `@label` as a whole value in a later step in place of the id the first step created. If the step created several objects, name the one you mean: `@label:msa`, `@label:senses`, `@label:codes`. Select a particular created phonological feature value with `@label:values:NAME`; a bare `:values` refuses if several values were created. Rule input, output and feature contexts resolve the same labels; a later step that needs the rule an earlier step created can name it with `@label:phonrules`.
- **There is no `@FEAT:` form.** A placeholder written `@FEAT:name` is not recognised: it stays as literal text and is then refused because it is not an id. A feature made in the same batch is reached by an `as` label on its `compose-author-exception-feature` step and `@label`. An existing feature has no placeholder at all: read its id from the project (`motif grammar read`) and write the id.
- **An allomorph shares its entry's analysis.** `compose-author-affix-process-allomorph` adds a form to the entry and does not create a second analysis, so one allomorph cannot carry a different tense or other label than the entry. To label two forms differently, make two entries, or add a second analysis with `compose-add-morphosyntax-analysis`.
- **Do not parse does not stop FieldWorks parsing.** Motif can mark an entry do-not-parse, but FieldWorks' HermitCrab, its XAmple transform and PanGloss all parse a flagged entry, so the flag is not a way to retire one. To stop a stem parsing, retype it with `compose-set-stem-part-of-speech` or delete it (see `compose-set-entry-do-not-parse`).

## Common wrong choices

- Reaching for an affix process, ad hoc prohibition or batch when a typed composer fits the claim.
- Making one large Proposal for several grammar questions.
- Describing an unmeasured change as an improvement.

entries.title: AI Handoff
entries.description: AI Handoff writes a folder you can share with a chat model. It includes project context for the words you parsed and a starter question. Settings shows what it plans to write and a data-sensitivity notice before you start; the folder can include real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences from the selected Texts.
entries.helpPage:
# AI Handoff

**AI Handoff** writes a folder you can share with a chat model. It includes project context for the words you parsed and a starter question. Settings shows what it plans to write and a data-sensitivity notice before you start; the folder can include real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences from the selected Texts.

Only one parse can run for a project at a time. A Handoff that needs a fresh parse runs it before writing. Motif refuses another parse request for the project until the Handoff finishes.

A Handoff requested for a traced word keeps the displayed trace and the Baseline captured with it. Motif does not parse the word again or make a replacement trace; this Handoff includes the raw diagnostic and leaves out measured results from a separate parse.

1. Open **Settings** at the bottom of the navigation rail. Turn on **Show Hand Off by Copying Files** and scroll to the Handoff controls. Read the notice. If it says the files will include only words chosen on the Texts page, choose **Hand off every parsed word instead** to use every word from the last parse.
2. Choose **Write the AI Handoff**. If you have already written one, the button says **Write the AI Handoff again**.
3. Choose an output folder when prompted and wait for Motif to finish writing.
4. Review the files, then drag the files into your chat or use the copy actions for the prompt and paths.

The utility shows when the files were last written and marks them out of date when a newer parse finishes. Times use your local clock; a timestamp from another day includes its weekday and date. The `read_results.py` reader works over `parse-results.json` and `texts.json`. Write the Handoff again when you want the chat model to receive newer results. Only share the files if you are comfortable sending their linguistic data to that service.

![AI Handoff files ready to share](shot:handoff-cancel-retry/completed-files)

A Handoff from a parse records refused words with a refusal code and reason in `parse-results.json`. Word forms use composed Unicode for reading and searching. `texts.json` is an empty array when no Texts were chosen; added words can still have measured parse results.

entries.title: Apply to FieldWorks
entries.description: In Proposals, open the Proposal you want to apply and read its Rationale and evidence. Choose Apply…. Motif activates that Proposal, reads its current review and checks whether Apply is available. Confirm Apply only when you want those changes written to FieldWorks.
entries.helpPage:
# Apply to FieldWorks

In **Proposals**, open the Proposal you want to apply and read its Rationale and evidence. Choose **Apply…**. Motif activates that Proposal, reads its current review and checks whether Apply is available. Before you confirm, the question names the backup: Motif does not back up your project, so back it up in FieldWorks first (**How to Back Up a Project in FieldWorks** opens FieldWorks' own help). Confirm **Apply** only when you want those changes written to FieldWorks.

Every change must still fit. The project's evidence and the Proposal's Trial must be current and complete enough for the engine's readiness rules. A held FieldWorks project, lost approved analysis, dropped grammar or an unresolved previous Apply can prevent writing. **Apply…** stays off, with its reason beside it, until the Proposal has a current Trial and ready evidence for your Selection; try it from the Proposals list first. Read the reason beside Apply and use **Refresh** or **Try Again** as appropriate. The window does not offer a force action.

A successful Apply shows the real Receipt. It makes the evidence of other open Proposals outdated, so measure them again before deciding. After an unconfirmed write, FieldWorks may already have these changes. Check the project and choose **Refresh** before trying Apply again. The window provides no post-Apply Undo; staged-change Undo applies only before changes have been applied.

entries.title: Parse all words
entries.description: Parse all words asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.
entries.helpPage:
# Parse all words

**Parse all words** asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.

While it runs, the progress panel stays visible at the top of the window. It shows how many words are done, the word currently being parsed, elapsed time and an estimate of the time left. It also shows the slowest word so far, with its parser work, and lists words that stopped at the work limit or the time safety net, each with its parser work. If no word finishes for a long time, the panel explains that the parser may have stalled and offers **Cancel** and **Report a problem**.

The result tells you which words parsed, which approved analyses PanGloss built again, and the time on this computer. Parser work gives a more stable measure for comparing grammar changes. A search that was interrupted or stopped at a limit is saved as not finished; it should not be read as a completed “no parse.” The **Progress** and **Texts** pages read the saved result. Opening either page does not run PanGloss.

After saving in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh** (the ⟳ beside the project name in the top bar) to read the saved project, then **Parse all words** in the project card to parse your [Default Selection](term:default-selection) again. A parse is evidence about one run, not a verdict that the grammar is good or bad.

Motif allows only one Parse all words run for a project at a time, even across windows and processes. If another window is already parsing that project, a second request is refused; use the running window to follow progress or cancel the run.

entries.title: Baseline
entries.description: A Baseline is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the .fwdata file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.
entries.helpPage:
# Baseline

A [Baseline](term:baseline) is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the `.fwdata` file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.

The Baseline is not a backup of linked media, and it is not a live view of FieldWorks. It stays in place until you capture another one. When a project has no Baseline, Motif captures one the first time you open it, then asks what to measure. Later, **Refresh** captures a new Baseline; **Parse all words** measures your chosen words against it. Opening a project with a Baseline reads it and the results already stored.

If the project has changed since the Baseline, Motif can mark its stored numbers as stale. A stale parse and a change that says **No longer fits** are related to different things: one is old measurement evidence; the other is a particular pending choice that no longer matches the project. See [Drift](term:drift).

entries.title: Cancelling a run
entries.description: During Parse all words, choose Cancel in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.
entries.helpPage:
# Cancelling a run

During **Parse all words**, choose **Cancel** in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.

Cancel keeps the results from the previous completed parse. The unfinished parse is not saved, and Motif does not change the FieldWorks project. For other long actions, use the **Cancel** control beside the running action: on **Why This Analysis?**, **AI Handoff**, or beside **Re-run chosen words** in **Timing**. The global progress panel also has **Cancel** while **Parse all words** runs.

![Parse all words progress and its Cancel control](shot:first-run-setup-parse/cancelling)

entries.title: Changing an analysis
entries.description: In Texts or Words, find the word, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. To keep one reading at several places of the same word, use the word panel described in Passage. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing an analysis

In **Texts** or **Words**, find the word, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. To keep one reading at several places of the same word, use the word panel described in [Passage](guide:passage). The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.

Each word has two buttons. The first is its opinion mark: **A**, **U**, **D**, or a dashed mark when FieldWorks holds no analysis. Choose **Set analysis** to see each stored analysis and choose **Set analysis: Approved**, **Set analysis: Unknown**, **Set analysis: Disapproved** or **Set analysis: Remove**, or to mark the spelling Incorrect. The current Opinion is shown without staging it again. Once you stage a change, the mark turns solid. The second button, **+** and a number, appears when PanGloss found analyses FieldWorks does not hold; choose **Add analysis from PanGloss** to add one as Approved or Unknown, or to add them all as Unknown. A chosen analysis shows **✓** and its number. Ctrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) undoes the last staged choice.

The change is kept as pending work for this project. It applies to the word form everywhere, not only the occurrence you were looking at. Open **Proposals** and look under **Your Changes Not Applied Yet** to inspect it. Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are choosing or reviewing.

To measure the effect before applying, open that document and choose **Check These Changes**. When you are ready, close FieldWorks and choose **Apply…**, then confirm. See [Apply to FieldWorks](guide:apply-to-fieldworks) for the conditions that must be met first.

## Inside a Proposal

When a Proposal is open, a word card adds a block called **In PanGloss · with this Proposal**. It shows the analyses PanGloss built for the word when the Proposal was last tried, and for each one the changes in the Proposal that built it. If the Proposal has not been tried yet the block says **Not tried yet**, while it is being tried it says **Trying…**, and if the project or the Proposal changed since, it says **Needs another try**. Nothing is tried again on its own.

Choose **Set analysis** to stage a change into the open Proposal instead of your pending word changes. **Approve … in** the Proposal's name approves an analysis FieldWorks already holds as Unknown that the Proposal now builds. **Add an expected parse to** the Proposal's name adds an analysis FieldWorks does not hold, as Approved, and the Proposal shows it as **Will add as Approved**. Either way the change is checked against the Proposal's own copy of the project, and it is applied together with the Proposal's other changes. If that copy has been cleaned up, the change is marked as needing another check; choose **Try again** on the Proposal bar.

Outside a Proposal nothing changes: your choices go to the pending word changes as before.

![A pending choice shown on its word card](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Default Selection
entries.description: The Default Selection is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each parse keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.
entries.helpPage:
# Default Selection

The [Default Selection](term:default-selection) is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each [parse](term:parse-all-words) keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.

The first time you set up a project, choose texts and add any extra words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?** Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to edit that choice later. The Selection needs at least one text or added word before Motif can parse. Setup, Settings, and **Analysis Options** in Texts → Sources edit the same saved parsing policy; see [Settings](guide:settings) for its time-limit choices.

The Default Selection is not a search query that changes behind your back. Motif resolves the chosen material for each run and records what it measured. After saving in FieldWorks, press **Refresh** to read the saved project, then choose **Parse all words** to measure the current Default Selection again.

The FieldWorks Text choices in **Texts → Sources** edit the current Selection. External Source **Context** changes instead stage a Proposal; **Current Chapter** stays local. See [Sources](guide:sources).

entries.title: Stale numbers and changes
entries.description: In the window, Motif marks a pending change as No longer fits when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.
entries.helpPage:
# Stale numbers and changes

In the window, Motif marks a pending change as [**No longer fits**](term:drift) when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.

For steps to check or remove a change, see **When a change no longer fits**.

entries.title: Choosing what to measure
entries.description: Motif measures words from the same texts and any added words each time, so its numbers can be compared from run to run. On a new project, Motif captures its first Baseline when you open the project, then opens setup. Setup takes four steps.
entries.helpPage:
# Choosing what to measure

Motif measures words from the same texts and any added words each time, so its numbers can be compared from run to run. On a new project, Motif captures its first Baseline when you open the project, then opens setup. Setup takes four steps.

On **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?**, choose one or more texts, or add words in the box labeled **Add Words:**. A long list of added words scrolls inside the box. Choose texts you have interlinearized: Motif compares its parses with the analyses you approved there. Words you add yourself are parsed too; if the saved project has an analysis for one, Motif can compare the parse with it. Choose at least one text or add at least one word to continue. On the Texts step and in **Texts → Sources**, choose **Select All Texts** to check every text. On a long list, choose **Clear** to uncheck them all.

On **How Much Work Should Each Word Get?**, set the **Parser Work Limit per Word**. The default is 20,000,000 parser work. You can change the shared parsing limits later as the **Parser Work Limit per Word** in **Analysis Options** in Texts → Sources, or Settings. **No Parser Work Limit** lets every word run to the end, which can take a very long time; you can still **Cancel**.

This becomes the project's [Default Selection](term:default-selection), the words Motif measures every time. **Start First Run** saves your choice and starts parsing; the progress panel shows how far it has got and stays on a final stage while Motif reads PanGloss's statistics. **Skip for Now** closes first-time setup without saving these choices and does not offer it again until you choose **Configure…**. **Cancel**, or Escape, also closes setup without saving; setup is offered again the next time the project is opened or refreshed. See [Settings](guide:settings) for the saved parsing policy.

Choose **Back** or **Next: Texts**, **Next: Limits**, and **Next: First Run** to move through setup.

![Choosing texts and added words in first-time setup](shot:first-run-setup-parse/selection)

After setup, open **Texts → Sources** to choose FieldWorks Texts or inspect external Source metadata. Paratext Source Context changes go through a Proposal; they do not import the external text into FieldWorks. See [Sources](guide:sources).

entries.title: Installing Motif
entries.description: Download the Windows x64 Setup.exe asset from the Motif Releases page, choosing the beta version named in your invitation. Beta downloads are marked as prereleases. Run Setup and follow the installer. It installs Motif for your Windows user and creates a Start menu shortcut. Launch Motif from that shortcut, then choose Select new… and browse to your FieldWorks .fwdata file. Motif reads your project and changes nothing in it until you choose Apply. Motif is a tech demo. Keep a FieldWorks backup and try it on a copy of your project first.
entries.helpPage:
# Installing Motif

Download the Windows x64 **Setup.exe** asset from the [Motif Releases page](https://github.com/sillsdev/motif/releases), choosing the beta version named in your invitation. Beta downloads are marked as prereleases. Run Setup and follow the installer. It installs Motif for your Windows user and creates a Start menu shortcut. Launch **Motif** from that shortcut, then choose **Select new…** and browse to your FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. Motif reads your project and changes nothing in it until you choose **Apply**. Motif is a tech demo. Keep a FieldWorks backup and try it on a copy of your project first.

The official Windows release includes the matching PanGloss parser. You do not need to download PanGloss separately.

Motif keeps workflow records in a file beside the FieldWorks project: for `Koro.fwdata`, the file is `Koro.motif.db`. It stores selections, pending changes, and measurement metadata; it is not a saved copy of the FieldWorks project. Motif does not currently support moving an existing project workspace: the database is bound to the `.fwdata` path and refers to files stored separately. Keep the project at its original path. The `.motif.db` alone is not a complete backup; include the `.fwdata`, `.motif.db`, and Motif worker root, which holds file-backed Baselines and parser artifacts. On Windows, the worker root defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SIL\Motif`; `MOTIF_WORKER_ROOT` can select another location.

Motif stops the PanGloss parser if it uses more memory than a limit, so one runaway word cannot take the rest of your computer's memory from other programs. The limit is 75% of the memory available to Motif (the container or cgroup limit when one applies). To change it, set the `MOTIF_PARSER_MEMORY_LIMIT` environment variable to a number of bytes, to a number with a binary suffix such as `12GiB`, or to `none`. `none` removes the limit; that is your choice to make, and while it is set one parser run can slow or crash everything else on the machine. Any other value is refused with a message naming the setting. A run stopped for passing the limit says so in its result; measure with fewer parser threads or a per-word parser work limit, or raise the limit.

Beta Windows builds may be unsigned. An unsigned Setup can show **Windows protected your PC** and **Unknown publisher**. Confirm that the version and download came from the Motif GitHub Releases page and match your invitation. If you trust that source, Windows may offer **More info** and then **Run anyway**; your organization's policy may prevent continuing. A signed build can also show a SmartScreen warning while it is new. If you cannot verify the download or Windows blocks it, ask the person running the trial for help. See [Microsoft's explanation of SmartScreen reputation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation).

The same release offers preview downloads for Linux x64 and macOS with Apple silicon. On Linux, make the AppImage executable and run it. On macOS, extract the portable ZIP and open the Motif app. These previews are not notarized macOS distributions or a promise of support for every Linux distribution. If your system blocks the preview, report the message to the person running the trial. An Intel Mac preview is not included.

Save in FieldWorks before **Refresh**; Motif reads the last saved project and can do that while FieldWorks remains open. Close FieldWorks before **Apply**. Motif refuses Apply if FieldWorks still owns the project.

Before 1.0, incompatible Motif stores are refused rather than upgraded. A confirmed **Delete Motif's store and reopen** recreates a refused project store and loses changes not applied yet. For damaged project or machine stores, follow [the recovery instructions](guide:when-something-goes-wrong); remove only the identified Motif file, never the FieldWorks project.

Motif keeps a local usage log of command names and argument shapes, not the supplied values. It has no usage-upload feature. Motif reads writing systems from the project's own files and the shared writing-system repository and makes no online language-tag lookups unless you set `MOTIF_SLDR_ONLINE=1`, so a machine without a network opens and checks projects; a language-tag cache already on the machine from the SIL Locale Data Repository may still be read. **Report a problem** lets you review a report that excludes project and language data by default; optional local details and AI Handoff files can contain private data, so review them before sharing.

Automatic updates are not enabled; download and install a newer release yourself. Uninstalling Motif removes its installation and command registration while leaving your FieldWorks project and Motif data in place.

entries.title: Affixes, slots, and templates
entries.description: An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A prefix comes before it, a suffix after it, and an infix inside it. As illustrative English examples, un-happy shows a prefix and kind-ness a suffix. The Turkish form evler (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to ev (“house”).
entries.helpPage:
# Affixes, slots, and templates

An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A **prefix** comes before it, a **suffix** after it, and an **infix** inside it. As illustrative English examples, *un-happy* shows a prefix and *kind-ness* a suffix. The Turkish form *evler* (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to *ev* (“house”).

Languages often restrict which affixes can combine and in what order. A **slot** is a position in that sequence. For example, an illustrative verb pattern might allow a person marker before a tense marker. Putting the same affixes in the reverse order could produce a form the language does not use.

In FieldWorks, affix templates organize slots for a part of speech. A noun template can describe noun patterns, while a verb template can describe verb patterns. Some slots are obligatory: a valid word using that template must fill them. Others are optional and may be skipped. These settings help the parser avoid treating every affix as freely combinable with every word.

When a trace reaches the right stem but stops before the expected ending, check the relevant template. Is the affix in the right slot? Is the order right? Is the slot required or optional as intended? Does the template apply to this part of speech? Keep one known word that should use the pattern and one similar word that should not; both help you check whether the template says what you mean.

The examples here are illustrative and simplified. Real languages can have several templates, and a slot can allow more than one affix.

entries.title: Allomorphs and environments
entries.description: One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are allomorphs. The conditions that choose between them are their environments: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.
entries.helpPage:
# Allomorphs and environments

One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are **allomorphs**. The conditions that choose between them are their **environments**: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.

Turkish vowel harmony is a useful real-language example. The plural suffix has the forms *-lar* and *-ler*. In the standard pattern, *-lar* follows a stem with a back last vowel, as in *okullar* (“schools”), and *-ler* follows a stem with a front last vowel, as in *evler* (“houses”). The forms belong to the same plural pattern; the stem’s vowel helps select which one fits.

A **natural class** groups sounds by a shared property, such as “front vowels” or “voiceless consonants.” Instead of writing a separate environment for every vowel, a grammar can use a natural class when the same condition applies to that group. This can make a rule clearer and easier to check.

When the parser builds the stem but cannot use the expected affix form, compare the allomorphs and their environments. Does the needed form exist? Does its environment mention the right sounds or features? Is the environment too narrow, so it misses a valid word, or too broad, so it allows the form where it does not belong?

The Turkish forms illustrate a common pattern; they are not a full account of Turkish. Real patterns may depend on additional features and exceptions.

entries.title: Help the parser work with your language
entries.description: You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.
entries.helpPage:
# Help the parser work with your language

You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.

The work is a loop:

1. **Measure.** Save your FieldWorks work, choose **Refresh**, then choose [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure words you care about. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) tells you how much of the chosen material parsed.
2. **Understand.** Open **Why This Analysis?** on a difficult word. Read the parser’s furthest attempt, then follow its steps to see what it built and where it stopped. Use **Timing** when words take a long time.
3. **Fix.** Use your language knowledge to check the likely cause. Make any grammar or lexicon change in FieldWorks, save it, then choose **Refresh** and **Parse all words** to measure again.

Motif's synthetic samples are generated to demonstrate its tools and give us small, safe places to practise. They are synthetic-turkic (Turkish-style), synthetic-bantu (Swahili-style), and synthetic-philippine (Tagalog-style), each modelled loosely on the named language. Their data are invented: they are not real language data and must not be used as descriptions of Turkish, Swahili, Tagalog, or any language.

You do not need to become a parser engineer to take part. You can tell an AI consultant what a word should mean and how it is built. Ask it to connect that analysis to the trace, suggest one small change, and name other words that should test the idea. Then check the suggestion against your language knowledge and Motif’s evidence. The AI can help with the machinery; it cannot decide what is right in your language.

entries.title: Modelling grammar in FieldWorks
entries.description: Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.
entries.helpPage:
# Modelling grammar in FieldWorks

Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.

## Start from the language

Write down what each part of your grammar means before you enter it: "the plural is *-ler* after front vowels and *-lar* after back vowels." Use examples from the language to check whether that description fits, including forms that show where the pattern does and does not occur.

## Sounds and spellings

Spelling and sound do not always line up one to one. When a pattern depends on a sound contrast, describe that contrast in the language and consider how the writing system represents it.

## Environments

An environment such as `/ [V] _` describes where an allomorph occurs. Use examples to identify the sounds or features around it, including contexts where a different form occurs.

## Allomorph order

When several allomorphs of one morpheme could fit, the first eligible one wins and blocks the rest. Put the most specific allomorph first and the general one last.

## Slots and templates

An inflectional template describes an order of affix slots. Decide which sequences occur in the language and which positions are optional, then compare the template with forms that illustrate those patterns.

## Features and classes

Features, their values, and inflection classes link by reference, not by name: two things with the same name are not connected. A noun-class system can use both an inflection class and a feature value for each class, as the synthetic Bantu-style sample does, but test agreement on real words before you rely on it.

## When a grammar is slow

When a parse takes longer than expected, use [Timing](cmd:timing) after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to inspect the time recorded on this computer. The Learn page **Why a grammar is slow** explains how to read Timing. Compare parser work when judging a grammar change.

## Change one thing at a time

After each change: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, then choose **Parse all words** before checking the words you expected to change, plus a few that shouldn't. One change per measurement tells you what each change did.

entries.title: Phonological rules
entries.description: When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonological rules

When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.

English plural endings give an illustrative example of a familiar sound pattern. The ending is usually pronounced with a voiceless [s] after a voiceless sound, as in *cats*, and with [z] after a voiced sound, as in *dogs*. After sibilant sounds, as in *buses*, an extra vowel is heard. These examples show how nearby sounds can affect the way an ending is pronounced; spelling alone does not show every sound detail.

A rule says what changes and in what environment. In plain words, one part of this pattern could be described as “make the ending voiced after a voiced sound.” A well-chosen rule covers the words that share that environment. A rule that is too broad can also change words you meant to leave alone, so check examples from both sides of the pattern.

Rule order matters when one rule changes something that another rule looks for. If Rule 1 creates the sound that Rule 2 needs to see, Rule 1 must apply first. If Rule 2 applies first, it cannot act on a sound that does not exist yet. When a trace shows an unexpected output, check both the rule’s environment and whether earlier rules have already changed the relevant sound.

You can change a rule after it exists: widen its environment, make an item in it optional or repeated, move it earlier or later, turn it off to see what the grammar does without it, or delete it. A rule's environment can name a word or morpheme boundary. Input and Output each hold up to eight phoneme or natural-class items in order; unequal lengths express shortening or lengthening, and an empty side means insertion or deletion.

## One rule, several outcomes

Wolff section 5.15 gives *kabukiran* and *kabukilan* from *bukid*: a lexically selected d alternates with r or l. A rule cannot express this free choice. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). Give each attested variant as an alternate form of the stem on the same entry, so there are no duplicate lexical entries. Keep rules for obligatory changes, with a literal or feature-class Output and a required exception feature on the selected stem analysis. Tag only the analyses supported by the source; this does not license *saylan* merely because *sayran* exists. The same holds for *lalum/lawum*.

Several right-hand sides serve a different purpose: they are ordered cases within one rule. Each has its own Output, left and right contexts, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. The first applicable case wins at a matching site. Two identical environments with d → r first and d → l second do not give free variation: the first hides the second. For optional lexical alternatives in one environment, use an Output class with the intended members, then check both forms in a Trial.

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) and [Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) let you keep several ordered cases in one rule, with lexical applicability per case. Read `motif help guide:encoding/phonological-rules --full` for the intent shape, expected-current guards and lexical alternatives. Rule features restrict applicability; they do not create an implicit dialect or register model.

entries.title: Reading why a word fails
entries.description: Why This Analysis? records the parser's search for the selected word. Turn on View → Diagnostics, select a word in Texts, open the grey fold in the word panel, and read the result.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading why a word fails

**Why This Analysis?** records the parser's search for the selected word. Turn on **View → Diagnostics**, select a word in **Texts**, open the grey fold in the word panel, and read the result.

Start with the result and search status:

- **Parsed** means a completed search found an analysis.
- **No parse** with **Search complete** means the search finished without finding an analysis.
- **Search incomplete** means the search did not finish. Read its recorded stop reason; an unfinished search is not evidence that no analysis exists, even when the trace contains no analysis.
- **Nothing to parse** means the grammar's character table does not define a character in the word.

Read any **Analysis summaries** before the **Recorded trace**. Expand tree context to see the recorded events. Select an event to read its exact input, output, raw reason code and captured rejection operands. A rule that was **Tried** was not necessarily **Applied**. **Blocked** names the recorded event without identifying an unrecorded blocker or treating it as the whole word's failure.

**Reason not recorded** and **Rejection details not recorded** mark missing evidence. A raw reason code is separate from the actual features or environment the parser captured. Do not infer a responsible rule from a nearby rejection or assume that every failed path explains the word's result. One attempt may fail while another succeeds.

**Grammar source not recorded** means the page cannot establish the trace's source save. **FieldWorks word context unavailable** means its stored analyses and opinions are unavailable here; it does not mean FieldWorks has no analysis. Use **Texts** on the result to read the word in its text. Use **Full derivation** for the complete recorded tree and filters. The diagnostic tools save the original trace independently of filters.

entries.title: Stems and the lexicon
entries.description: The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.
entries.helpPage:
# Stems and the lexicon

The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.

As an illustrative English example, *walk* is the stem, *to move on foot* is a possible gloss, and *verb* is its part of speech. The form *walked* can be built from that stem and a past-tense ending. A gloss is a short guide for people, not a complete definition or a promise that two languages divide meaning in the same way.

One of the most common causes of failure is a missing stem. If a grammar expects to start with *walk* but that stem is absent or entered under a different form, adding the ending rule will not give the parser a starting point. In a simplified, illustrative Turkish example, the stem *ev* (“house”) is needed before the grammar can analyse *evler* (“houses”) with the plural suffix.

When a word fails, compare the form you typed with the lexicon entry you expect. Check spelling and the relevant writing system, then check that the entry has the stem and part of speech your analysis requires. If the stem is there, move on to the affixes and rules that should build the rest of the word.

The examples here are illustrative; real entries and analyses depend on the language and the choices made in its FieldWorks project.

entries.title: What the parser knows
entries.description: A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current Baseline. It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.
entries.helpPage:
# What the parser knows

A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.

A **parse** is an analysis the grammar can build for a word. As an illustrative English example, *cats* can be analysed as the stem *cat* plus the plural ending *-s*. The parser must find a matching stem and a permitted way to combine it with the ending. A word can have more than one possible analysis, and a completed search may find none.

“It doesn’t parse” describes the result for this word and saved grammar. To judge whether that grammar matches the language, compare the result with the forms and patterns speakers use.

First check whether the search completed. A completed search with **No parse** tells you the grammar did not produce a reading. **Search incomplete** means the parser stopped before finishing, so it cannot show that the grammar has no possible analysis. A search may stop at the work limit (its analysis-parser work limit or the derived work limit), at the time safety net or for another cause. If the record does not identify which it reached, Motif keeps that reason general. A word with a character missing from the grammar’s character table is a different case again.

The parser reports what its grammar allowed. You decide whether that grammar matches the language.

entries.title: Why a grammar is slow
entries.description: A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Why a grammar is slow

A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.

An optional slot lets the parser consider a form both with and without that slot. Broad environments let a rule apply in many places, creating more possible continuations. An empty affix adds no visible letters, so the parser can add it without consuming part of the word, though PanGloss often handles these cheaply: in the synthetic Bantu-style sample, 160 empty allomorphs added no measurable work. A duplicated real affix is different; there, copying one object marker into a second slot multiplied the work.

Use **Diagnostics → Speed by Rule** after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to locate recorded parser work. Each rule's steps are divided by the exact measured-word count shown above the table. The unattributed remainder stays visible. Partial per-word detail is labelled; missing counts stay unavailable. A rule's work shows where steps were spent, not what caused a word to parse or stop. Select a rule to open its verified FieldWorks destination.

Check that each optional slot is truly optional, each environment names the sounds it should, and each affix appears only where intended. Read and edit rules in FieldWorks. Change one thing at a time and measure again. The [Timing command](cmd:timing) offers recorded work outside the window as well. No Fast or Slow threshold is inferred from a rule's count.

entries.title: Working with an AI consultant
entries.description: You bring knowledge of the language. An assistant can suggest a Proposal for you to review. Motif supplies recorded evidence, and you decide whether a proposed change fits.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with an AI consultant

You bring knowledge of the language. An assistant can suggest a Proposal for you to review. Motif supplies recorded evidence, and you decide whether a proposed change fits.

Use **Ask Claude** on a word or warning to record a Request with your optional note. **Claude** in the top bar shows Requests waiting for a Proposal and links to setup in Settings. It has no embedded conversation or live Claude connection indicator. Use Claude in its own application. See [Ask Claude](guide:ask-claude) and [Connect an assistant](guide:ai-assistants).

Ask a focused question about the word, the recorded evidence and examples that should still fail. Treat the answer as a hypothesis and check it against what speakers say and use. Edit rule definitions in FieldWorks; Motif shows names and available **Open in FieldWorks** links.

Review a returned Proposal on **Proposals**. A Request never Applies it. You review the evidence and choose whether to Apply a Proposal yourself.

For a file-based exchange, turn on **Show Hand Off by Copying Files** in Settings. Read the data-sensitivity notice, choose the write action, then review the files before sharing them. Motif does not upload them for you. See [AI Handoff](guide:ai-handoff).

entries.title: Opening a project
entries.description: Open the project menu and choose Select new… to browse for a FieldWorks .fwdata file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose Open recent and select it, or choose it from the list on the initial Choose a project page. The window opens on Progress and shows the results from the last run. Opening a project doesn't parse anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Opening a project

Open the project menu and choose **Select new…** to browse for a FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose **Open recent** and select it, or choose it from the list on the initial **Choose a project** page. The window opens on **Progress** and shows the results from the last run. Opening a project doesn't parse anything.

On **Choose a project**, each recent row shows its recorded state and wordform count when those details are available. **Refresh needed** means the saved project is newer than those results. **Open folder** opens the folder containing the project without opening the project in Motif; you can reach the link with Tab and activate it with Enter.

You can also choose a FieldWorks backup, a `.fwbackup` file. Motif restores it into a new folder beside the backup, named after the project, and opens that copy, so the backup itself is never changed. If a folder of that name is already there, Motif uses the next free name, such as `Koro 2`, and leaves the earlier copy as it was.

If this project has no Baseline yet, Motif captures one when you open it and then opens setup. Later, press **Refresh** to read the project as FieldWorks last saved it. Save your latest edits in FieldWorks first if you want them included: unsaved edits in FieldWorks are not part of the file Motif reads. You do not have to close FieldWorks just to open a project. If another program is using the project, Refresh may say “the project 'Koro' is in use by another program” (using your project’s name); close the other program and try again.

On a new project, Motif captures the first Baseline and asks which words to measure. See [Choosing what to measure](guide:first-run-setup).

entries.title: Progress and project health
entries.description: Progress shows supported next actions for the open project. A Proposal appears as a next action when its stored standing says it is waiting for a decision. If there is no supported action, the page does not invent one.
entries.helpPage:
# Progress and project health

**Progress** shows supported next actions for the open project. A Proposal appears as a next action when its stored standing says it is waiting for a decision. If there is no supported action, the page does not invent one.

Open Requests can also appear as next actions; they record what a person asked and do not imply a connected Claude session.

The health strip shows available stored project facts. Its details can include a recorded median parser-work value; the face does not show parser-step counts. Warnings and timing details are available in **Diagnostics** when it is enabled. Opening Progress or the health details reads stored information and does not start a parse.

After saving in FieldWorks, use **Refresh** to read the saved project. Run the parser when you want new results for the current Selection. See [Reading project health](guide:reading-the-overview) for how to interpret the available facts.
