The page uses plain Next rows with ordinary keyboard activation. See [Progress](guide:progress) for their destinations and unavailable states. Parse completion is separate from approval at a place in a text; chapter approval and weekly activity are not shown without their own recorded evidence.

entries.title: PanGloss
entries.description: In Texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its analyses with what FieldWorks stores.
entries.helpPage:
# PanGloss

In Texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its analyses with what FieldWorks stores.

PanGloss parses the project's grammar. Motif records parser warnings and refusals alongside the results.

For a FieldWorks Opinion, A means Approved, U means Unknown, and D means Disapproved. An empty dashed box in the FieldWorks Opinion position means no analysis is stored. In Texts, ≠ with a solid underline marks a new or different PanGloss result; ∅ with a dashed underline means no parse, and ◖ with a dotted underline means a stopped search. These PanGloss cues are separate from the FieldWorks Opinion, and their glyphs and line styles carry meaning alongside color. Staged means a choice is waiting for **Apply**.

![The compact word strip for geldi](shot:explained-word-card/approved-agrees)

entries.title: Pending Changes
entries.description: Changes staged from a word stay pending until a person applies them. Open Proposals to inspect the pending document and its Comments and evidence. Staging does not write changes to FieldWorks.
entries.helpPage:
# Pending Changes

Changes staged from a word stay pending until a person applies them. Open **Proposals** to inspect the pending document and its Comments and evidence. Staging does not write changes to FieldWorks.

## Keeps staged from the Passage

Keeping a reading in **Texts**, whether with Enter, Shift+Enter or **Approve** in the word panel, stages one pending change for each place. Each change records the word, the place it belongs to and the reading you chose, and a place shows as staged only after its change has been written. Keeping the same reading at a place that is already staged does nothing, so nothing is staged twice.

A keep of a reading that only the parser offered is a new analysis. FieldWorks creates it only when you choose **Apply**, and it is still your decision until then. Before applying, open the pending document in [Proposals](guide:proposals), which lists the staged changes by Text. Proposals has no button to undo one; to take back the last staged choice, press Ctrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) in the window.

If a keep is refused, the sentence beside the word panel or in the status line says why, and no place that was not written is shown as staged.

**Undo** and **Redo** (Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y, ⌘+Z and ⌘+Shift+Z on macOS) affect staged changes only, one staging action at a time, and the window has no on-screen Undo button. Before applying, check that the changes still fit the project and explicitly measure what they do. Missing or outdated evidence is not a successful check. See [Apply to FieldWorks](guide:apply-to-fieldworks) and [When a Change No Longer Fits](guide:when-a-change-no-longer-fits).

entries.title: Reading project health
entries.description: The health strip reports facts available from the saved project and stored results. A warning is a finding to inspect, not an instruction to change the grammar. Open Diagnostics when enabled to read stored warnings and rule timing.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading project health

The health strip reports facts available from the saved project and stored results. A warning is a finding to inspect, not an instruction to change the grammar. Open **Diagnostics** when enabled to read stored warnings and rule timing.

Parser work measures the work recorded by the parser. It is distinct from elapsed time on a particular computer. A missing or stale measurement does not mean that the parser did no work; Motif leaves unavailable health facts out. The median, when recorded, is in the health details.

Opening these views does not run the parser. After saving in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh** to read the saved project, then parse the current Selection when you need new results. See [Progress and project health](guide:overview).

The Progress page’s Next rows open waiting Proposals and open Requests. Their counts come from stored records, and rows disappear while those records are read again. Neither parser completion nor a wordform’s approved analysis proves that a person approved every occurrence. See [Progress](guide:progress).

entries.title: The Motif window
entries.description: The window has five main pages: Progress, Texts, Words, Grammar Guide, and Proposals. Choose a page in the rail on the left. Settings stays at the bottom of the rail.
entries.helpPage:
# The Motif window

The window has five main pages: **Progress**, **Texts**, **Words**, **Grammar Guide**, and **Proposals**. Choose a page in the rail on the left. **Settings** stays at the bottom of the rail.

**Progress** shows available project facts and next actions. **Texts** opens the reader and the current Selection. **Words** lists the words in the whole Context. **Grammar Guide** reads the project's saved Grammar Design Records. **Proposals** shows saved Proposals and their standing, rationale, and Comments.

Each page owns its controls and any side panel it needs. In a narrow window a side panel can fold away; use its labelled reveal to open it again. The window adapts as you resize it or change zoom.

The health strip shows the project facts that are available. Open its details by hovering over it or moving keyboard focus to it. When a recorded median parser-work value is available, it appears in those details. Opening the strip does not start a parse.

Diagnostics is off by default. Turn it on from the health details or **View → Diagnostics** to add **Diagnostics** to the rail. Its two tabs show recorded grammar **Warnings** and **Speed by Rule**. Turning Diagnostics off hides the page and returns to Progress if it was open.

[Settings](guide:settings) contains display preferences, project options, assistant connections and the optional file Handoff. For keyboard navigation, see [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts).

entries.title: Building a grammar: a suggested order
entries.description: This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. Motif does not check, enforce or remember where you are in it, and nothing in the window is greyed out or reordered by it. Motif has no setting for the type of language, and FieldWorks has none either. Work in whatever order your language and your data suggest, and go back to any part when a test shows a gap.
entries.helpPage:
# Building a grammar: a suggested order

This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. Motif does not check, enforce or remember where you are in it, and nothing in the window is greyed out or reordered by it. Motif has no setting for the type of language, and FieldWorks has none either. Work in whatever order your language and your data suggest, and go back to any part when a test shows a gap.

The method follows H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 3 July 2025), which ships in the FieldWorks 9 Help. Black organises his guide by mechanism, not as a numbered procedure. The order below is our reading of his tips and worked examples, so where it says "Black §2.1.1" it names the section that supports one step, not a sequence he sets out himself. Lessons from our own grammar builds are labelled **In our experience**; they are not from Black or from any textbook.

Black states the goal this way: "The idea is to use the morphotactic mechanisms to correctly describe the facts of the language and thereby not only provide correct parses, but also rule out false parses" (§2, opening). So the aim is a grammar that parses what is a word and does not parse what is not. Neither Black nor Motif sets a percentage to reach.

You make grammar and lexicon changes in FieldWorks. Motif shows what the parser did with them: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, then [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure again.

## Texts and words to test on

**What to do.** Choose some Texts you have interlinearized, and add any extra words you care about. This is your [Default Selection](term:default-selection), the words Motif measures every time. Mark spellings you know are not words as Incorrect spelling.

**Why.** Texts give you real words to test every later step against, and measuring the same words each time lets you compare one run with the next. Fieldwork textbooks place connected texts alongside the rest of the work: Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork* (2nd ed., 2015), has a chapter titled "Discourse, Pragmatics, and Narrative Data" (chapter 9).

Our own suggestion, which has no source: Motif measures only the Default Selection, so you can leave one Text out of it and add it later to see how the grammar does on words you did not tune it to.

**In Motif.** Setup asks you to choose texts or add words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?**; choose **Configure…** from the project menu to change it later (see [Choosing what to measure](guide:first-run-setup)). In **Texts** or **Words**, choose **Set analysis** on a word and mark its spelling Incorrect; the change stays pending until you review and apply it in **Proposals** (see [Texts](guide:texts) and [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts)).

## Sounds

**What to do.** Define the phonemes and natural classes before anything refers to them. If you will use phonological rules, give the phonemes features too; Black's worked example creates the features, makes sure every phoneme is defined, assigns the features, then writes the rules.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 says environments for allomorphs are defined "once the set of phonemes and natural classes are defined", and §3.1.1 says you need a list of all the phonemes to use environments or natural classes. For the rule-based parser, §6.2.1 says every phoneme used in the orthography must be defined, and a word with even one undefined phoneme is "guaranteed to not give an analysis"; §6.2.2 says features must give each phoneme a distinct set of values; §6.2.3 and §6.2.4 say to be as specific as practical. Black's worked example in §6.1.2.1.4.1 (Figure 51) runs: create the features, make sure every phoneme is defined, assign the features, then write ordered rules. The fieldwork textbooks also take sounds first: Bowern's chapter 5 is titled "Fieldwork on Phonetics and Phonology", before chapters 6 and 7 on morphology and syntax.

**In Motif.** A word PanGloss cannot read shows **PanGloss can’t read it** with its recorded reason. If the reason names the project’s phonemes, inspect the phoneme inventory before parsing again (see [Texts](guide:texts)). **Why This Analysis?** traces the selected word (see [Why This Analysis?](guide:why-this-analysis)).

## Words and their parts

**What to do.** Work out the morphemes by comparing forms, for example, forms that share a part with the same meaning. Enter roots, stems and affixes as lexical entries, each with the right morpheme type. When you know whether an affix is inflectional or derivational, say so.

**Why.** Black §1.2 lists what a parser must know: the forms and glosses of prefixes, infixes, roots and suffixes, which affixes go with which roots, their relative order, and when a shape is legitimate. For a word made of one morpheme, §2 says to add a lexical entry and set the morpheme type of its allomorph to a root or stem type; §4.2 lists the morpheme types the parser keys on. On classification, §2.1.1 says an unclassified affix "is relatively unconstrained as to where it can appear", so the parser may return incorrect parses, and "the best solution, of course, is to classify the affix as being either inflectional or derivational". §2.1.5 gives criteria for deciding (Bickford's table) and adds that they "are not hard and fast rules". Label an affix unclassified when you do not know yet, and change it when you do.

**In Motif.** Parse your Selection and open **Progress**. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) says how many of your chosen words parse. Read it as one measure among several: it is not a score for the grammar (see [Reading project health](guide:reading-the-overview)).

## Where affixes go

**What to do.** Give each category its templates and slots, so affixes appear only in the positions they can occupy.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.1 to §2.1.2.5 cover templates, optional slots, multiple templates, discontinuous morphemes and the interaction with categories. Black's Morphotactics section (§2) opens by saying morphotactics controls the order of morphemes and which can co-occur.

**In Motif.** After a change in FieldWorks, parse again and open **Why This Analysis?** on a word that should contain the affix. It shows what the parser built and where it stopped.

## Allomorphs

**What to do.** When one morpheme has several shapes, decide what chooses between them. If a sound environment does, use a phonological environment. If it is a lexical property of the stem, use an inflection class. If it tracks something the word agrees with, use a feature.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 and §3.1.4 cover environments and allomorph ordering; §2.1.2.6 inflection classes; §2.1.2.7 agreement and other inflection features; and §2.1.2.8, Table 9, offers guidelines for choosing between a class and a feature. Order here is ours: Black explains environments in his morphophonemics section and classes and features in the morphotactics section.

**In our experience.** Give each stem its class as you add it. In a Tamil build, a restriction that limited a past-tense suffix to one inflection class made nine types that had parsed stop parsing, because two verb stems had no class yet. Eight parsed again once those two stems were given the class (Tamil checkpoint report).

**In Motif.** The **Lost** list in **Texts** marks a word FieldWorks holds an Approved analysis for that the grammar no longer builds (see [Texts](guide:texts)).

## Agreement

**What to do.** Put the features on the words that are agreed with, and then on the affixes that agree with them. The order is ours; Black §2.1.2.7 shows the mechanism, not a sequence.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.7 uses Spanish gender to show how inflection features rule out incorrect parses, and Table 8 lists situations where features can do the same.

**In our experience.** In a Swahili build, adjective concord was entered with noun-class features required on the affixes (proposal 0133) before nouns carried the feature (proposal 0134). The build log records that a mismatched noun and adjective could not be shown to fail until the nouns had it (Swahili build report). Later, of the 523 tokens in an annotated sample that a reference marked as real words but the grammar did not parse, 174 needed concord series for function words, the second-largest group after missing lexemes (206). The reference was drafted with AI help and has not been reviewed by a native speaker (Swahili gap report).

## Stem alternations and exceptions

**What to do.** For stems or affixes whose shape changes in ways sound environments do not explain, condition the allomorphs on morphosyntactic features. For single combinations that are simply wrong, mark the exception.

**Why.** Black §3.7 covers non-phonologically conditioned allomorphy, with stem allomorphs and affix allomorphs conditioned by features; §3.8 covers irregularly inflected forms; §2.1.6 covers exception "features", for stems and affixes that combine incorrectly "due to historical or some other seemingly arbitrary reasons".

## Derivation, compounds and clitics

**What to do.** Add derivational affixes, compound rules and clitics once the inflection beneath them is working.

**Why.** Black covers derivational affixes in §2.1.3, stem compounding in §2.2 and clitics in §2.3. The ordering is ours; Black does not say to do these after inflection.

## Ordered phonological rules

**What to do.** Write phonological rules once you have stems and affixes to test them on.

**Why.** Black §6.1.2 notes that these rules are ordered, so that the output of one is the input to the next, and §6.2 lists the checks that make the rule-based parser work. The sequence "once there are stems and affixes to test them on" is ours.

**In Motif.** **Why This Analysis?** lists the rules on the best path of a trace, and says that **Tried** does not mean **Applied** (see [Why This Analysis?](guide:why-this-analysis)).

## Ad hoc rules, last

**What to do.** Use an ad hoc rule only when a wrong parse persists after you have used the other mechanisms.

**Why.** Black §2.4 says to use them "when one has used all the mechanisms provided by the parser to the best of one's ability and such incorrect parses continue to surface"; §3.10 says the same for allomorph-oriented rules.

## Keep null morphemes few

Black §4.1.1 says one "wants to avoid having null allomorphs if for no other reason than that they can make the parser run rather slowly". If a null allomorph is the best analysis, keep it. The **Timing** page shows which words are slow.

## How this varies by type of language

Motif has no typology setting, and FieldWorks has none either. A language's type shows in its grammar, in what you end up needing: templates and slots for rich affixation, affix processes for reduplication or infixation, compound rules, inflection classes and features for agreement systems, and phonological rules where sounds change at morpheme boundaries. A language with little inflection may never need most of these steps; a language with heavy agreement will spend most of its time in the Agreement section. Black's guide has sections for reduplication (§3.2), infixation (§3.3), epenthesis (§3.4), metathesis (§3.5) and incorporation (§2.2.3).

## Optional checks

You may also list a whole closed class, such as all the demonstratives or all the pronouns, and check that each parses. You may also lay out a paradigm table for one stem and look for empty cells. Motif does not measure either one; the checks are yours to run with **Why This Analysis?**.

## Going back

The order loops. Testing shows gaps in earlier work, and Black says as much about affix classification: "as you study the language more, you should eventually figure out whether such affixes are inflectional or derivational" (§2.1). Return to any part when a Parse all words shows a gap. The same holds for false parses: when a word you know is not a word parses, go back to the part that lets it through.

## Further reading

- H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 2025), in the FieldWorks 9 Help.
- Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork: A Practical Guide* (2nd ed., 2015), chapters 5 to 9 and Appendix B, "Suggested Fieldwork Programme for an Undescribed Language".
- Eugene A. Nida, *Morphology: The Descriptive Analysis of Words* (1949).
- The Rapid Word Collection method (rapidwords.net), for gathering vocabulary by semantic domain.

entries.title: Refresh the project
entries.description: Use Refresh after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif to read that saved state. Refresh captures a new Baseline and checks the grammar for Warnings. It does not parse words. Choose Parse all words after Refresh to measure the current Default Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Refresh the project

Use **Refresh** after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif to read that saved state. Refresh captures a new [Baseline](term:baseline) and checks the grammar for **Warnings**. It does not parse words. Choose [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) after Refresh to measure the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection).

1. Save your work in FieldWorks.
2. In Motif, choose **Refresh** (the ⟳ beside the project name in the top bar) and let it finish.
3. If setup opens after the first Baseline, choose what to measure and press **Start First Run**. Otherwise, open the project card (choose the project name in the top bar) and choose **Parse all words**.
4. Check **Progress**. Refresh updates the project counts and checks the grammar; parsing updates the parse results.

If you cancel **Parse all words** or the parser refuses it, Refresh's new Baseline remains; parse results do not describe it until a parse completes. Opening Motif again does not refresh a project that already has a Baseline.

![Refresh captures a Baseline before a separate parse updates the numbers](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/refreshed)

entries.title: Replace a Pending Change
entries.description: Return to the word in Texts and undo the staged choice you want to replace. Read its current context before making another choice. Undo affects staging only and does not reverse an applied Proposal.
entries.helpPage:
# Replace a Pending Change

Return to the word in **Texts**. Press Ctrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) to take back the last staged choice, or stage the new choice for the same place. There is no on-screen Undo button, and Ctrl+Z takes back only the most recent staging action. Read the word's current context before making another choice. **Undo** affects staging only and does not reverse an applied Proposal.

After replacing a staged change, measure the exact new content again before applying. Earlier evidence does not establish readiness for the replacement. Read [Pending Changes](guide:pending-changes) and [Apply to FieldWorks](guide:apply-to-fieldworks).

entries.helpPage:
# Switching projects

Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.

1. Choose **Select new…** to browse for a `.fwdata` file, or choose **Open recent** and select a project Motif already knows.
2. Wait for the project’s Baseline, Selection, and stored results to load.
3. Check the project name on **Progress** before taking an action.

Each project has its own Motif workflow information. Switching away does not move its pending changes into another project; when you open it again, its changes are shown with that project. If Parse all words or AI Handoff is running, switching projects cancels that work before Motif loads the new project.

Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to reopen the project’s saved Selection and parsing limits. Use **Refresh** to read the saved project and capture a new Baseline, then choose **Parse all words** to measure the saved Selection; opening the project alone only reads stored results.

entries.title: Text Coverage
entries.description: Text Coverage measures how much of the Default Selection produced a completed parse in the saved results. The Overview command reports selected words and their places separately: one written form can appear many times in a Text.
entries.helpPage:
# Text Coverage

[Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) measures how much of the Default Selection produced a completed parse in the saved results. The [Overview command](cmd:overview) reports selected words and their places separately: one written form can appear many times in a Text.

Parse completion is not human approval. It does not establish that a person kept an analysis at each place. Progress does not use this measure to fill a chapter approval strip or calculate an approval percentage.

A completed search with no analysis differs from an incomplete search that stopped at a work limit or the time safety net. Missing, unreadable or stale results do not mean zero. Digit-only places and places in other writing systems are counted separately where the stored Text summaries provide those counts.

The command can also group recorded parse coverage by frequency band. A word list's supplied counts describe that list, not places in a Text. Choose **Texts** to inspect the current Selection's words and places, and see [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) for the stored run's scope. See [Progress](guide:progress) for the window's Next rows and health details.

entries.helpPage:
# Texts

**Texts** shows the reader and the current Selection in **Sources** and **Passage**. Open the side panel to inspect Paratext Source metadata or choose **FieldWorks Texts**. Check the FieldWorks Texts to include in the current Selection, then choose a Text in the reader to open its Passage and available analyses. Opening Texts does not start a parse.

Selecting a Paratext Source shows its saved Context, local folder and Current chapter. External Passage text is unavailable; Motif does not substitute a FieldWorks Text with the same name. See [Sources](guide:sources) for the supported kinds and the difference between Source, Context and Current.

Choose a word to inspect its recorded analysis and available actions, and to see every place the word occurs in the word panel; see [Passage](guide:passage). To inspect the word rows for the whole Context, open [Words](guide:words). To save the material measured for future runs, configure a [Default Selection](guide:default-selection).
